story: In August 1877, astronomer Asaph Hall discovered Deimos using the US Naval Observatory's 26-inch refracting telescope. Named after the ancient Greek god of dread, Deimos is the smaller and outer of Mars's two irregular moons, spanning roughly 12 kilometers across. Lacking sufficient mass for gravity to pull it into a sphere, Deimos consists of dark, carbon-rich rock covered in a smooth layer of porous regolith. Because of its tiny mass, Deimos has an extraordinarily weak gravitational pull, with an escape velocity of just 5.6 meters per second—around 13 miles per hour. That means an athletic human sprinting on its surface could easily launch themselves straight off into space. Furthermore, while its sibling moon Phobos is spiraling inward toward a catastrophic collision with Mars, Deimos is slowly drifting outward, destined to eventually escape Mars's gravity and wander interplanetary space alone.
angle: Deimos has an escape velocity of just 5.6 meters per second (13 mph), meaning a human sprinting across its surface could leap straight off the moon and float into space.
disputed: Origin of Deimos: Sources dispute whether Deimos is a captured C- or D-type asteroid, formed in situ from impact ejecta debris, or originated from the disruption of a common parent moon with Phobos. Handle by attributing: 'scientists still debate whether Deimos is a captured asteroid or re-accreted impact debris.'
